title: Git Exercises
description: Practise the ideas from this Git course. Each answer has an explanation to help you learn.

exercises.question: Does local Git require a GitHub account?
exercises.explanation: Version control records changes over time. Git can work on your own computer without a hosting service. The command reports the installed Git version. If Git is missing, use its official installation guide with a trusted adult.

exercises.question: What does git init create here?
exercises.explanation: A repository is a project whose history Git tracks. Initialise only a new practice directory for this lesson. Git creates its hidden .git directory inside learning-git. That directory holds the repository information.

exercises.question: What does untracked mean?
options: Git has not added the file to its tracked history
exercises.explanation: The working tree is the set of files you edit. status tells you what is new, changed or ready for a commit. Git reports note.txt as untracked because it has not yet been added. The printf command is for a POSIX-style shell such as Git Bash.

exercises.question: Which command reviews staged changes?
exercises.explanation: The staging area holds the changes you intend to put in the next commit. Add only the files you mean to include. The staged difference shows note.txt ready for the next commit. Reviewing it helps avoid accidental additions.

exercises.question: What does a commit record?
exercises.explanation: A commit records the staged snapshot with a message. Git needs a name and email label, which are part of the commit metadata. The local repository records the staged note. These labels are for this practice repository, not a login.

exercises.question: What does a plus line usually show in a diff?
exercises.explanation: A diff shows how current content differs from another version. Review it before saving the next version. The difference shows the added second line. Lines with a plus are additions in the displayed comparison.

exercises.question: What does git log show?
exercises.explanation: The log lists commits. The short view helps you see their order and messages without opening each snapshot. The log shows the saved commits. HEAD names the current checked-out commit in this normal branch workflow.

exercises.question: What does switch -c do?
options: Create and switch to a branch
exercises.explanation: A branch is a movable name pointing to a line of commits. It lets you work on a change without immediately adding it to another branch. Git creates and switches to club-note. Start from a clean working tree so unrelated edits do not confuse the exercise.

exercises.question: Who decides the intended text in a real conflict?
exercises.explanation: A merge joins histories. If two branches change the same lines differently, Git may need a person to choose the result. The graph helps you see branch history. Merging is a decision about changes, not a way to hide conflicts.

exercises.question: Does .gitignore erase old committed secrets?
exercises.explanation: A .gitignore file lists patterns Git should ignore when files are not already tracked. It is useful for temporary output. The untracked scratch.log is ignored. The .gitignore file itself can be tracked.

exercises.question: What is a remote?
exercises.explanation: A remote is a named address for another repository. Viewing remotes does not upload or download commits. A new local repository may show no remotes. This is normal and does not stop local commits.

exercises.question: What makes a shared change easier to review?
options: A clear purpose and focused difference
exercises.explanation: A good shared change has a purpose, a reviewed difference and a short explanation of checks. A hosting service can review it separately from local Git. The change is easy for another person to understand. Publishing it is a separate deliberate action.
